column4: The traveler is repeatedly told to look at preserved food, his donkey, and the bones as God raises and clothes them; an enacted resurrection is placed directly before the reflective eye.
Abraham asks to be shown how God revives the dead, and the birds make that act perceptible so his heart may be reassured; it joins visible demonstration to inward certainty.
God shows Abraham the dominion of the heavens and earth so that he may become certain, a positive realization of the invitation in 7:185 to inspect that dominion.
Abraham sees a star and tests whether a visible heavenly object can be Lord; its setting begins a disciplined gaze that refuses to stop at the object.
He then sees the rising moon and again lets its setting expose the insufficiency of appearances, continuing the skyward examination begun in 6:76.
The sun, greater and brighter, is subjected to the same observed rising-and-setting test, so even the eye's grandest object cannot be the final destination of sight.
Abraham turns his face toward the One who originated the heavens and earth; it states where the created-object gaze of 6:75-78 is meant to lead.
The viewer sees mountains and supposes them fixed while they pass like clouds; God's perfected workmanship corrects a confident surface judgment about the very object faced in 88:19.
After the second trumpet blast, people are suddenly standing and looking; resurrection restores them to sight only within the compelled scene of the Last Day.
The Prophet's gaze neither swerves nor exceeds its bound during the great vision, supplying a positive model of an eye both free of humiliation and exact in attention.
He sees some of his Lord's greatest signs, completing 53:17's disciplined gaze with the true perception of signs that empty looking lacks.
وَالسَّمَاءَ رَفَعَهَا states that God raised the sky and established the balance, directly matching the upper object and action posed in 88:18.
وَالْأَرْضَ وَضَعَهَا لِلْأَنَامِ turns from the raised sky to earth laid down for creatures, closely matching the vertical movement of 88:18-20.
أَلَمْ تَرَوْا كَيْفَ خَلَقَ اللَّهُ asks viewers how God created seven layered heavens, a repeated formulation of the section's creation-question.
Moon and sun are placed within those heavens as light and lamp, giving the upward gaze of 71:15 definite visible objects.
God caused humanity to grow from the earth like a plant, joining the observer's creation to the ground being observed.
God will return people into earth and bring them out again, making the earth-growth of 71:17 an explicit image of burial and resurrection.
أَلَمْ نَجْعَلِ الْأَرْضَ مِهَادًا opens another creation proof by asking about earth made as a prepared resting place.
The mountains are made as pegs, completing the precise earth-and-mountain pair of 78:6 and closely echoing 88:19-20.
Seven strong heavens are built above, adding the upper direction to the earth and mountains of 78:6-7.
A blazing lamp is placed in the built heavens, giving the eye a familiar sign within the upper structure of 78:12.
Abundant water is sent from rain clouds, beginning the visible provision that follows the earth-sky construction.
Grain and vegetation emerge by that water, showing what the prepared earth yields beneath the raised sky.
Dense gardens complete the inspectable sequence begun with earth in 78:6 and rain in 78:14.
At the upheaval, prized pregnant she-camels are abandoned; the animal people are asked to inspect now loses all ordinary value when the promised Day arrives.
أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا asks whether people see that God created livestock for their possession, a close animal-creation counterpart to the camel question.
The livestock are subjected so that some are ridden and some eaten, exposing the fitted relation between the animal's created form and human use.
Benefits and drinks come from those animals, then أَفَلَا يَشْكُرُونَ names gratitude as the proper answer to seeing how they were made serviceable.
God made cattle so people may ride some and eat some; the camel's observable form is read through the purposes built into it.
Cattle meet needs in people's breasts and carry them alongside ships, extending 40:79's fitted animal-human relation.
God shows His signs and asks which they deny, explicitly naming the livestock scene of 40:79-80 as something displayed for recognition.
The Creator makes pairs and provides ships and cattle to ride, bringing created animal form into a wider order of transport.
Settling on their backs should prompt remembrance of the One who subjected them; ordinary riding becomes reflective seeing of fitted creation.
The riders confess that they will return to their Lord, carrying the contemplation of cattle in 43:12-13 through to final return.
Every earth-creature and flying bird forms communities like human beings and will be gathered to the Lord, joining animal observation to resurrection.
There is an instructive lesson in cattle: pure milk is brought from within their bodies, directing thought through an animal's familiar exterior to hidden making.
Cattle contain a lesson, drink, benefits, and food; their created usefulness is itself offered for contemplation, closely paralleling the camel's invitation.
Hearing, sight, and heart are each accountable, so the present ability to look at creation is a responsibility rather than a neutral possession.
Those God leaves astray are gathered on their faces blind, dumb, and deaf; this intensifies the section's lowered eye into total bodily and sensory abasement.
Those gathered on their faces toward Hell are called worst in place and way, a Last-Day reversal of today's upright, ranging observation.
God brings living from dead and dead from living, revives earth after death, and says that likewise people will be brought out.
Winds, heavy clouds, rain, and dead land bearing fruit culminate in كَذَٰلِكَ نُخْرِجُ الْمَوْتَى, an indirect creation scene made explicit as resurrection evidence.
Rain revives earth after its death and is called a sign for those who hear, pairing the visible revived ground with receptive perception.
Lightning, hope and fear, rain, and revived earth are signs for people who understand, joining upward sight and downward life in one observable process.
Measured rain revives a dead land, followed by كَذَٰلِكَ تُخْرَجُونَ; the landscape supplies a direct image of human emergence.
The heaven is built with power and made vast, a compact counterpart to the question how the sky above was constructed.
The earth is spread out immediately after 51:47's heaven, reproducing the section's downward turn from raised sky to laid ground.
أَلَمْ نَجْعَلِ الْأَرْضَ كِفَاتًا asks about earth made as a container, another direct question about the prepared ground under the viewer.
The earth gathers both living and dead, giving 77:25's containing ground a relation to present habitation and burial.
High firm mountains and fresh water are placed on that earth, completing a close mountain-ground-water counterpart to 88's viewed landscape.
God makes earth a settlement and sky a structure, then forms people well; the observer, upper world, lower world, and created form are gathered in one claim.
The human was a drop of emitted fluid, beginning another answer to the question how a familiar creature was created.
The drop becomes a clinging form which God creates and proportions, exposing the hidden sequence behind the visible human observer.
Male and female are made as a pair from that formation, completing the first-creation account.
The passage asks whether the One who performed 75:37-39 can revive the dead, drawing the same return-inference from how creation began.
أَوَلَمْ يَرَ الْإِنسَانُ asks whether the human sees that God created him from a drop, turning the viewer's own origin into the contemplated object.
The human forgets his creation and asks who can revive decayed bones, stating the failure of thought that 36:77 exposes.
The answer points to the One who originated the bones the first time, making first creation sufficient evidence for return.
Fire produced from green trees supplies another visible reversal of states before 36:81 turns to creation of heavens and earth.
Garden companions are described as قَاصِرَاتُ الطَّرْفِ; restrained sight here belongs to purity and ease, not the compelled humiliation of the lowered Last-Day gaze.
The repeated قَاصِرَاتُ الطَّرْفِ places voluntarily bounded eyes within Garden companionship, preserving a positive form of lowered gaze.
Garden companions whose glances are restrained show that visual constraint can signify exclusive attention, a boundary distinct from furtive fear or disgrace.
A covering lies over their sight after heart and hearing are sealed; exposed objects cannot produce perception when the receptive faculty is closed.
Those cursed for turning away are made deaf and their eyes blinded, turning moral refusal into the loss of the very faculties needed to receive signs.
Jacob's eyes turn white from grief as he suppresses sorrow; the physical eye named by عين loses sight through suffering, unlike the freely ranging eye of the section.
When the bearer of good news casts the shirt over Jacob's face, he becomes seeing again; restored sight makes the organ's vulnerability and gift palpable.
They hurry with fixed attention toward the Caller and name it a hard day; this supplies the summons and judgment to which the lowered eyes of 54:7 respond.
At the siege, eyes swerve and hearts reach throats; earthly terror already shows sight displaced from calm, deliberate movement.
The unexpected expulsion leaves a lesson for أُولِي الْأَبْصَارِ, making visible historical collapse something people of insight must read.
Every soul is told to look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow; نظر becomes present self-examination oriented toward the Day before sight is compelled there.
ثُمَّ نَظَرَ uses the section's contemplative sense of نظر for a hostile evaluator of revelation, showing that mental scrutiny can still be bent toward a false verdict.
On the near punishment's Day, a person looks at what his hands sent ahead; the reflective act postponed in life becomes unavoidable self-review.
Faces that Day are radiant, supplying another half of the opposing Last-Day face tableau that structures surah 88.
Those radiant faces laugh and rejoice, completing the blessed face-state introduced in 80:38.
Other faces that Day are covered with dust, a direct counterpart to the humbled face and downward association of 88:2.
Darkness overspreads the dust-covered faces of 80:40, completing their visible mark of ruin.
The dust-darkened faces are identified as disbelieving and flagrantly sinful, stating the moral division expressed visually in 80:40-41.
The traveler reaches the sun's setting-place and finds it setting at a spring; عين as spring and an act of skyward seeing meet in one perspectival scene.
Recognizing the truth heard from the messenger makes their eyes overflow with tears; bodily eyes register inward perception rather than empty looking.
God spreads earth, casts firm mountains into it, and grows everything in measure, closely restaging the lower two objects viewed in 88:19-20.
Earth is made a cradle with paths, rain descends, and diverse paired plants emerge, giving the downward gaze both traversable ground and signs of making.
God makes earth a carpet for people, continuing 71:15-18's creation-and-return sequence with the ground's present usability.
Broad roads through that earth explain how people may move across the surface they are invited to inspect.
The gloomy face of 75:24 expects a back-breaking calamity; this ayah supplies the anticipation that visibly shapes the face.
At one blast people are suddenly looking, another resurrection scene in which sight resumes only after the decisive summons.
